name: Pre-Offer Rehab Review
title: Free Pre-Offer Rehab Review for Investors | Genstone
metaDescription: Send a property you are evaluating and get a repair estimate, a refined ARV and a clear read on whether the numbers support your offer before you commit.
lede: The cheapest time to find out a rehab does not work is before you own the house. Genstone Construction's complimentary Pre-Offer Rehab Review estimates the repair costs on a property you are evaluating, refines the after-repair value, and tells you whether the repairs and projected resale or rental economics support the offer you are considering. You get real repair numbers before you commit capital, not after demolition starts.

sections.h2: Why the review happens before the offer
sections.body:
Most investor losses are baked in at acquisition. The purchase price was set using a repair number that turned out to be optimistic, an after-repair value that assumed a finish level the budget could not deliver, or a quick walkthrough that missed a failing foundation, a dead sewer line or a roof with nothing left. By the time the problem shows up, the capital is committed and the options are narrow.

The Pre-Offer Rehab Review moves the hard questions to the front of the deal. Before you make an offer, our estimators look at the property and give you a repair estimate grounded in what renovations actually cost, an after-repair value tied to the scope that estimate covers, and a direct answer to whether the numbers support the price you have in mind.

We offer it at no cost because it is how good projects start. Investors who know their rehab numbers before they buy make better acquisitions, and better acquisitions become renovations that run smoothly. Some reviews turn into Genstone projects. Others lead the investor to renegotiate or walk away, and that is a good outcome too, because a deal avoided is capital preserved for the next one.

The review is useful across every strategy we support: fix and flip, BRRRR, single-family rental acquisitions, small multifamily buildings of two to four units, and bank-owned properties. The questions change somewhat by strategy, and the review is shaped to the way you plan to use the property. It is also useful for comparing several candidate properties and putting your offer behind the one with the clearest path to the return you need.

The more we know, the sharper the review. You do not need everything on this list, but each item narrows the uncertainty in the estimate.

- The property address and the listing, if there is one.
- Photos and, if you have one, a video walkthrough. Interior photos of the kitchen, baths, basement or crawlspace, attic, mechanical equipment, electrical panel and water heater are especially helpful, along with the roof and exterior from each side.
- The price you are considering offering and the asking price.
- Your strategy for the property: resale, BRRRR, long-term hold or owner-occupant financing such as FHA 203(k).
- The comparable sales or rents you are using, if you have already pulled them.
- Any seller disclosures, prior inspection reports, appraisals or repair bids.
- For small multifamily buildings, the rent roll, unit mix and which utilities are separately metered.
- For bank-owned properties, whether utilities are on and whether the house has been winterized.
- Your lender's draw and rehab requirements, if the purchase is financed.
- Access details and your timeline for making a decision.

Photos of the systems matter more than photos of the finishes. A dated kitchen is easy to price from a picture. A water heater label, an electrical panel, a stained ceiling under a bathroom or a foundation wall with a horizontal crack tells an estimator far more about the real budget.

Send what you have through the Pre-Offer Rehab Review form or call (312) 429-2637. If the deal is moving quickly, tell us your offer deadline.

The review answers three questions: what the house will cost to renovate, what it will be worth when the renovation is done, and whether those numbers support your offer.

The repair estimate breaks anticipated costs into meaningful categories rather than a single lump sum. Systems are separated from finishes, so you can see how much of the budget goes to the roof, structure, plumbing, electrical, heating and cooling, and how much goes to kitchens, baths, flooring, paint and exterior work. Debris removal is accounted for. Items that cannot be confirmed from the information available are identified as open risks rather than guessed at.

The ARV refinement ties the after-repair value to the scope. An ARV is only meaningful in relation to a particular finish level. A house renovated with a light refresh is compared against different sales than the same house with a full kitchen and bath renovation. We look at the comparables you are using, or the ones that fit the scope, and tell you whether the value you are assuming matches the house the budget will produce.

The bottom line is a direct read on the deal. Given the repair estimate, the refined ARV and the strategy you described, do the numbers support the offer you are considering? If they do, you go forward with more confidence. If they do not, the review shows where the gap is, whether it is a repair item that could be negotiated, a value assumption that is too high, or a price that needs to come down.

For rental strategies, the same logic applies to the rent the finished property can command and the value a refinance appraisal is likely to support.

sections.h2: Multiple ARV plans for the same house
sections.body:
Many properties support more than one reasonable renovation. The right choice depends on the comparables, your budget, your timeline and your strategy, and the only way to choose well is to see the options side by side. Where it helps the decision, the Pre-Offer Rehab Review prices more than one plan.

A typical comparison might look like this:

- A light plan: correct what a buyer's inspection or a rental inspection would flag, refresh paint, flooring and fixtures, and leave sound original features in place. Lower cost and fewer days, aimed at the value-minded end of the comparables.
- A market plan: renovate the kitchen and baths to match the bulk of the renovated sales or rental comps nearby, along with the systems work the house needs.
- A full plan: reconfigure the layout, add a bathroom or bedroom where the comps show buyers or renters paying for it, or carry the finish level to the top of the neighborhood.

Each plan pairs a scope and cost with the ARV it is designed to support. Seeing them together lets you compare the added cost of each step against the added value, and weigh the extra time each step adds to the project. Sometimes the full plan clearly earns its cost. Often the market plan delivers the best balance. And sometimes the light plan is right because the neighborhood will not pay for more.

Multiple plans also help in negotiation. If the deal only works at the light plan, you know your margin for error is thin and can set your offer accordingly. If even the light plan leaves room, you know you can compete harder for the property.

A credible repair estimate is one of the strongest tools an investor has when negotiating. Sellers and listing agents discount vague claims that a house needs a lot of work. They take a specific, itemized estimate from a renovation contractor more seriously.

There are several ways investors use the review at the negotiating table:

- Setting the initial offer. Working backward from a supported ARV and a real repair number gives you a maximum price grounded in the property rather than a rule of thumb.
- Asking for a repair credit or price reduction. If the review identifies major items the listing did not disclose, such as a roof at the end of its life or a failing sewer lateral, those items can justify a lower price.
- Prioritizing inspection items. When your inspection contingency is running, the review tells you which findings matter most and roughly what they cost, so you negotiate on the items that move the numbers.
- Competing with confidence. In a multiple-offer situation, knowing exactly how much room the deal has lets you bid aggressively on a property that works and step back from one that does not.
- Walking away. If the numbers do not work at any price the seller will accept, the review gives you a clear reason to move on.

How much of the estimate to share with the seller's side is your decision. Some investors share the full line-item estimate to support a price reduction. Others summarize the major items. Either way, the review gives you specifics to point to.

The review is also useful outside negotiation. Lenders and partners often want to see a repair estimate before committing to a deal, and an itemized estimate from a contractor carries more weight than a spreadsheet assumption.

sections.h2: What a pre-offer review can and cannot see
sections.body:
A pre-offer review is a disciplined estimate based on the information available before you own the property. It is not a substitute for a full home inspection or a specialist evaluation, and it is honest about where its uncertainty lies.

Some conditions are easy to assess from photos and a walkthrough: the age and style of kitchens and baths, flooring condition, paint, visible exterior issues and the general layout. Others are harder. Conditions hidden behind walls, under floors and in buried lines cannot be seen without opening them up. Mechanical systems may appear intact but fail when tested. On bank-owned houses, the utilities may be off, which hides plumbing leaks and electrical problems until the systems are restored.

The review identifies those open risks rather than ignoring them. Where an item cannot be confirmed, we say so and explain what would confirm it. Common next steps include a full home inspection, a sewer camera inspection on older houses with original lateral lines, a roof inspection, a structural evaluation where cracking or settlement is visible, or testing for lead-based paint or asbestos in older homes where renovation will disturb painted surfaces or old flooring and insulation.

When the deal justifies it and access is available, a site walk by one of our estimators adds a great deal to the accuracy of the review. Seeing the house in person allows a closer look at the systems, the structure and the details photos miss.

You can also account for uncertainty in your own numbers. Where the review identifies meaningful open risks, carrying a contingency in your underwriting is sensible, and the review helps you size it to the specific risks of that house.

sections.h2: From review to project, or to the next deal
sections.body:
If the numbers work and you buy the property, the review becomes the starting point for the renovation. After closing, we schedule a full site walk, confirm or adjust the review's findings with the house open and accessible, and prepare a detailed scope document and estimate with anticipated labor and materials, debris removal included, and a draw schedule. Where you asked for multiple ARV plans, you choose the plan, and the scope is built around it.

A designated field manager is assigned to the project from start to finish. Genstone coordinates vetted, licensed and insured local contractors from a national network of thousands. Permits, inspections, lien waivers and contractor compliance are handled as part of the project, and you can follow progress, documentation and milestones without being on site. No upfront payment is required, construction draws are tied to completed work, final payment follows completion and your approval, and finished work carries a one-year workmanship warranty.

If the numbers do not work, the review has still done its job. You keep the estimate, the ARV analysis and the list of open risks, and you can use them to negotiate, to reconsider the property at a different price, or simply to move on. There is no obligation to hire Genstone because you requested a review.

The Genstone Companies can support the rest of the acquisition where you want them to: Genstone Financial for fix-and-flip, DSCR rental and construction loans, Genstone Realty for acquisition and off-market opportunities, Genstone Insurance for vacant and rental coverage, and Title Clearing & Escrow for closing. Send your next property to start a review.

faqs.q: Is the Pre-Offer Rehab Review really free?
faqs.a: Yes. The Pre-Offer Rehab Review is complimentary. We offer it because investors who understand their rehab numbers before buying make better acquisitions, and better acquisitions lead to renovations that run well. Some reviews turn into Genstone projects, and some lead investors to renegotiate or pass on a property. Either outcome is useful, and requesting a review does not obligate you to hire us.

faqs.q: What do I need to send for a review?
faqs.a: At minimum, the address and the price you are considering. Photos, especially of the mechanical systems, electrical panel, water heater, basement or crawlspace, roof and any visible damage, make the estimate far more accurate. Helpful extras include the listing, your strategy, the comparables you are using, seller disclosures, prior inspections, and for small multifamily buildings, the rent roll and utility setup.

faqs.q: How accurate is a pre-offer estimate?
faqs.a: It is as accurate as the information available before you own the property allows. Finishes and visible conditions can be priced reliably. Hidden conditions, such as damage behind walls, buried sewer lines or systems that cannot be tested, are flagged as open risks with the inspections that would confirm them. A site walk by one of our estimators, when access is available, improves accuracy considerably.

faqs.q: What is a multiple ARV plan?
faqs.a: It is a comparison of more than one renovation approach for the same house, each with its own scope, cost and the after-repair value it is designed to support. A light plan, a market plan and a full plan are a common set. Seeing them side by side lets you weigh the added cost and time of each step against the added value before setting your offer price.

faqs.q: Can I use the review to negotiate with the seller?
faqs.a: Yes, and many investors do. An itemized estimate from a renovation contractor gives you specifics to support a lower price or a repair credit, particularly when the review identifies major items the listing did not disclose. It also helps you prioritize inspection findings and decide how hard to compete in multiple-offer situations. How much of the estimate you share with the seller's side is up to you.

faqs.q: Does the review replace a home inspection?
faqs.a: No. The review is an investor-focused repair estimate and ARV analysis, not a full home inspection. It identifies the conditions most likely to affect your budget and points out where a home inspection, sewer camera inspection, roof inspection, structural evaluation or environmental testing would reduce uncertainty. Many investors use the review to decide whether a property deserves a full inspection in the first place.

faqs.q: Can you review bank-owned or multifamily properties?
faqs.a: Yes. The review covers single-family homes, small multifamily buildings of two to four units, and bank-owned properties. For multifamily buildings, we pay particular attention to shared systems, unit configuration and legality. For bank-owned homes, we look for the conditions common in vacant properties, such as freeze damage, mold and stripped systems, and note where utilities being off limits what can be confirmed.
